title: Tsutomu Yamaguchi — the man who survived both atomic bombs
sources: Wikipedia: Tsutomu Yamaguchi (16 March 1916 – 4 January 2010) — Nagasaki-born draftsman for Mitsubishi Heavy Industries designing oil tankers; in summer 1945 on a three-month business trip to Hiroshima; on 6 August he was leaving with colleagues Akira Iwanaga and Kuniyoshi Sato, on his way to the station, when he realised he had forgotten his hanko and went back; at 8:15 he was walking towards the docks about 3 km from where Little Boy exploded; he recalled seeing the bomber and two small parachutes before 'a great flash in the sky, and I was blown over'; ruptured eardrums, temporary blindness, serious burns on the left side of his upper body; spent the night in an air-raid shelter, returned to Nagasaki the next day; reported for work heavily bandaged on 9 August; at about 11:00 he was describing the Hiroshima blast to his supervisor, who called him 'crazy', when Fat Man detonated, his workplace again about 3 km from ground zero; unhurt by the blast this time, but fever and vomiting for over a week; recognised as a hibakusha of Nagasaki in 1957; officially recognised as a survivor of both bombings on 24 March 2009, the only person so recognised, though at least 160 people are known to have been affected by both; later campaigned for nuclear disarmament, including at the United Nations in 2006; died of stomach cancer on 4 January 2010, aged 93

Photos (public domain, Wikimedia Commons / US National Archives / US Air Force / US Navy): the atomic clouds over Hiroshima and Nagasaki; Enola Gay; Bockscar; Hiroshima from the air, August 1945; Hiroshima Station after the bombing; Nagasaki before and after; Nagasaki ruins in the Urakami valley; the Mitsubishi Nagasaki dockyard (pre-war postcards)
Archive film (public domain): 'Tale of Two Cities' (US War Department, Army-Navy Screen Magazine no. 74, 1946) — B-29s, Hiroshima and Nagasaki after the bombings — illustrative, not Yamaguchi himself
Portrait photograph of Tsutomu Yamaguchi (not public domain; supplied by the user, used for identification) and an illustrated portrait (labelled on screen as an illustration)

post.facebook:
He survived the atomic bomb on Hiroshima. Three days later, he was standing under the second one.

Tsutomu Yamaguchi was a Mitsubishi engineer from Nagasaki, sent to Hiroshima for three months in the summer of 1945. On 6 August, his last day, he went back for his forgotten personal stamp. At 8:15 he saw a bomber and two small parachutes — then a great flash. About 3 km from the blast, his eardrums burst, he was blinded for a time and badly burned.

The next day he took the train home to Nagasaki. On 9 August, wrapped in bandages, he went back to work and was telling his boss how one bomb had destroyed a whole city. His boss called him crazy. Then Fat Man exploded over Nagasaki — again about 3 km away.

For decades Japan recognised him only as a Nagasaki survivor. In 2009 he became the only person officially recognised as surviving both bombings, though at least 160 people are known to have been caught in both. He spent his last years campaigning against nuclear weapons, and died in 2010, aged 93.

Luckiest man alive, or the unluckiest? ☢️

youtube.description:
He survived the first atomic bomb. Three days later, he was standing under the second.

Tsutomu Yamaguchi, a Mitsubishi engineer from Nagasaki, was on a business trip to Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 — about 3 km from the blast. Burned and half-deaf, he took the train home to Nagasaki, went back to work in bandages on 9 August, and was telling his boss about the bomb when Fat Man exploded, again about 3 km away. In 2009 he became the only person officially recognised by Japan as a survivor of both bombings. He died in 2010, aged 93, after years of campaigning against nuclear weapons.
